notable_claims: Copyright violation is not viewed as a free speech issue by university and corporate administrators.
Lawyer's letters to feeder sites like UUNET could effectively shut down specific newsgroups without formal lawsuits.
The public perception of USENET as a 'pirate network' could lead higher-ups at institutions to lower their opinion of the net overall.
classification.summary: Brad Templeton discusses the potential for copyright holders to pressure USENET administrators into censoring 'pirate' newsgroups via lawyer's letters. He argues that universities and corporations would likely comply to avoid trouble, potentially leading to a broader perception of the network as a pirate haven. This could result in increased censorship or lawsuits against system administrators.
classification.title: Where pirate groups could lead us...

identity.subject: Where pirate groups could lead us...

notable_claims: Fair use is defined by statute, rule, and case law, not by the copyright owner.
Posting entire newspaper articles to USENET is generally not considered fair use.
Most USENET 'included quotes' likely constitute fair use as they facilitate debate with an author.
classification.summary: Brad Templeton provides a detailed explanation of the 'fair use' doctrine in US copyright law to clarify common misunderstandings on USENET. He emphasizes that fair use allows for limited copying for purposes such as criticism, news reporting, and education without the owner's permission. The post specifically addresses the legality of quoting materials in online debates and warns against posting entire works.
classification.title: What "Fair Use" is

notable_claims: Students at York University were fighting disciplinary actions related to anti-semitic statements.
classification.summary: Carl M. Kadie provides a pointer to the CAF-batch archive regarding a dispute involving students at York University facing disciplinary action. The discussion centers on whether speech containing anti-semitic statements is protected or subject to university discipline.
classification.title: York Students Fight Racist Discipline

identity.subject: Re: [alt.activism] York Students Fight Racist Discipline

notable_claims: A federal jury found that a professor's speech was a motivating factor in his removal as department chairman.
The court held that the expectation of disruption is insufficient to justify removing a leader without proving they are ineffective regardless of the speech.
classification.summary: A federal jury awarded professor Leonard Jeffries $400,000 in damages after finding that the City University of New York (CUNY) violated his First Amendment rights. The court ruled that CUNY's decision to remove Jeffries as chairman of the black studies department was motivated by a controversial speech he gave in 1991.
classification.title: CUNY to pay $400,000 free speech violation

identity.subject: [UPI] CUNY to pay $400,000 free speech violation

notable_claims: Censorship of any kind is never to be taken lightly as it sets precedents that can later be used against the censors.
The U.S. Supreme Court declared 'Fanny Hill' not obscene in 1966.
classification.summary: Jon Noring defends the distribution of a hypertext version of 'Fanny Hill' after David White requested its removal from various archives based on policies against adult material. Noring argues that censorship sets dangerous precedents and asserts that the work is a literary masterpiece protected by legal standards. The exchange highlights early internet debates over content moderation, archive policies, and the tension between community standards and free expression.
classification.title: Censorship of Fanny Hill (was Re: Unsuitable upload: please delete)

notable_claims: The electronic version of 'The Hacker Crackdown' was released as literary freeware.
The book is available via the CAF/WELL whatsnew server and EFF archive servers.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie provides instructions for accessing the electronic version of Bruce Sterling's book, 'The Hacker Crackdown: Law and Disorder on the Electronic Frontier'. The text notes that the book is being released as 'literary freeware' and can be accessed via Gopher or email through EFF servers.
classification.title: _The Hacker Crackdown_ on-line
